The declaration of a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) was created by the International Health Regulations (2005) and is WHO's highest level of alert for a health emergency. PHEICs are declared by the WHO Director-General on the basis of a recommendation provided by the International Health Regulations (IHR) Emergency Committee. This paper challenges the orthodox thinking around PHEIC declarations, using a methodological approach that has not been used in this space, through a series of interviews with those involved in the PHEIC declaration process.

When taking into consideration the historical origins of IHR and global health security paradigm, it is not surprising why the main criteria for referring an event for in-depth assessment and consideration as a potential PHEIC emphasize containment at the source, with particular concern given to unknown events with high-risk of international spread. These elements reflect the enduring tradition of health regulations that prioritize containment over prevention, a legacy that continues to shape global health responses. Additionally, data from the WHO public health intelligence report indicate that countries in the global South remain the primary sites of verified alerts. No longer being a PHEIC does not mean COVID-19 is not a pressing problem anymore. The WHO Director-General has emphasized the need for implementing sustainable long-term public health strategies. Gaps in vaccination rates across multiple countries continue to pose a risk of severe infections. Considerable uncertainties remain related to the impact of long-COVID on the global burden of disease for the years to come.

But, at the same time, there is no quantitative threshold for determining when an event is no longer “unusual or unexpected”. As explained in the previous paragraph, the spread of wild poliovirus continues to be a PHEIC despite its nine-year duration. The main reason, in this case, is the persistent “risk of international spread” of the disease. The point can thus be made that it lies within the discretion of Emergency Committee members, and ultimately of the WHO Director-General, to interpret when exactly these criteria are met. Aiming for a mathematical threshold marking a before-and-after is a vain undertaking. Much like the first declaration of a PHEIC due to COVID-19 from over three years ago, the recent declaration of the end of a PHEIC does not entail any before-and-after in the overall legal status quo.
